newsitem.title: INDIA: Wary India firms take harder look at GDR plans.
newsitem.headline: Wary India firms take harder look at GDR plans.

text.p: Indian companies, wary despite a 15 percent jump in Bombay's benchmark stocks index this year, are taking a harder look at the market before committing themselves to global equity issues, analysts said on Tuesday.
"There's a strong feeling that though there is some substance in the current rally, there's also a fair amount of froth," said Rupa Bose, strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in Singapore.
Bombay's benchmark stocks index has surged 15 percent in 1997 and is up 31 percent from a three-year low in December.

"People are waiting for things to stabilise. It's embarrassing if you start out on an issue and the market plummets by 300 points in one day," Bose said, referring to the recent volatility across stock exchanges.
Prices have risen sharply on frequent assurances by the government that it will soon announce an economic package to boost capital markets. The measures are expected this week.
"We are optimistic that the rally will last, but not cocksure," said Seshadri Ratnam, finance director of Bharti Enterprises.
Group firm Bharti Televentures plans to raise around $200 million through an issue of American Depositary Recepits (ADR) around April.
"One needs to wait for some more time," Ratnam said.
Indian companies raised around $1.6 billion in 1996 through Global Depositary Receipts (GDRs) and convertible bonds against less than $400 million in 1995.
Analysts say companies are especially nervous after fledgling telecom firm BPL Cellular in December withdrew its $200 million ADR issue -- India's first U.S. equity offering.
BPL said it was forced to withdraw the issue due to "negative sentiment" towards Indian stock.

"Most of the Indian companies either don't want to go because they perceive that their share price is still too low or because they are nervous of failure," said Shaun Browne, director, equity capital markets, at HSBC Investment Bank.
"They are also waiting to see if the government issues work. The last private company that tried (BPL) got a very bloody nose," Browne said.
Two mega issues totalling around $800 million are due from state-run telecom firm Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL) and India's largest refiner Indian Oil Corp (IOC).
Analysts say VSNL will be the first company to approach the international market this year with its issue of GDRs scheduled for February. IOC's issue is due in March.
"The government issues have crowded out the market. Unless these go private players don't have the courage," said the head of corporate finance at a European investment bank.
Private companies waiting to launch global equity or equity-linked issues include Hutchison Max, Bharti Televentures, Dabur, SPIC, Modi Luft and IPCL.
Analysts said recently announced takeover guidelines -- which made the procedure more transparent -- were another source of worry.
"Most promoters are now keen to have as large a stake as they possibly can. Anything that is going to dilute their holding is not what they want," HSBC's Browne said.
"Many of them are just sitting tight and using internal accruals or resorting to project finance," he said.
